problem: Classical navigation stacks (mapping, localization, cost-function planning) struggle to turn open-ended, semantically rich language commands (e.g. 'follow the person carefully', 'avoid obstacles') into motion without hand-crafted costs or task-specific training. Diffusion navigation policies such as NoMaD plan in opaque latent spaces that a human cannot inspect before execution.
motivation: The motivating observation is that if a generative video model can render a realistic video of the robot doing the task, it has in effect already solved the planning problem (UniPi, GAIA-1, and the authors' earlier FlightDiffusion for UAVs). Explicit generated videos also give a human-readable plan that can be checked before execution. The paper asks whether this 'video-as-planning' idea carries over to ground and legged robots driven by nothing more than a single scene image plus a language prompt.
key_idea: Refine the user's prompt with a VLM, have a world foundation model (Cosmos 2.5) 'dream' a third-person video of the robot doing the task, then geometrically recover the robot's trajectory from the generated frames (YOLO detection → IPPE-PnP → EKF → world frame) and execute it on the real robot.
insight: The whole pipeline is training-free apart from a small robot detector: semantics come from frozen foundation models, and metric structure comes from classical geometry (known robot dimensions and PnP). This decoupling lets one pipeline run unchanged on a wheeled UGV and a quadruped. Generating a third-person view is argued to reduce ambiguity in localizing the robot, but no ablation tests this claim, the refinement step, or any other component. The failure analysis is informal: failures come from generated videos that misrepresent the scene layout and from accumulated pose-estimation error, so the geometric-extraction stage is the weak link.
method: Prompt refinement: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (zero-shot) takes the initial frame I0 and the raw instruction. It performs scene grounding, resolves references such as 'there' or 'it', and decomposes motion into metric/directional primitives, e.g. 'moves forward at 1 m/s, curving left 30° to avoid the chair'.

Video generation: NVIDIA Cosmos 2.5 runs latent diffusion conditioned on the refined-prompt embedding and the initial-frame embedding to produce N RGB frames. It is conditioned on an elevated third-person camera viewpoint (TPV) so the robot is visible within the global scene.

Robot detector: YOLO11n trained on a small hand-annotated dataset of real lab images plus diffusion-generated images (some with hallucinated robots) of both UGV and quadruped platforms, so it works on real and generated frames.

Pose recovery: keypoints inside the bounding box are matched to a simple 3D model built from the known robot dimensions. IPPE-based PnP with camera intrinsics K gives the robot position in the camera frame. ORB-SLAM3 estimates the virtual camera pose per generated frame.

Temporal filtering: an EKF with a constant-velocity model (6-D state of position and velocity, position-only measurement) smooths the PnP positions. Positions are then transformed to the world frame with the estimated camera pose.
Execution: the 3D trajectory is projected onto the ground plane as a 2D reference curve, which the physical robot tracks open-loop. Execution is recorded with VICON for evaluation.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (frozen) + NVIDIA Cosmos 2.5 video world model (frozen) + YOLO11n detector (trained) + ORB-SLAM3 / IPPE-PnP / EKF (classical)
setting.training_data: No training of the planner (VLM and video model used zero-shot). YOLO11n is trained on a small custom dataset of real lab robot images plus diffusion-generated images, manually annotated with bounding boxes; dataset size not reported.
setting.observation: single third-person RGB scene image showing the robot and targets, plus a natural-language instruction
setting.action_space: 2D ground-plane reference trajectory (sequence of (x,y) points) extracted from the generated video, tracked by the robot's controller
setting.privileged: Known robot physical dimensions (3D model for PnP) and camera intrinsics; requires a third-person image with the robot visible. VICON motion capture is used only for evaluation.

numbers_note: Evaluation is only a small custom real-world study (3 tasks × 10 trials in a VICON lab), with no standard benchmark and no baselines. The paper states Table 1 contains 'approximate performance values read from the reported plots'. Final/tracking errors compare the generated plan with the VICON-executed trajectory, not the true goal location. The success criterion and generation latency are not reported. The 'split' field is set to 'test' only as a placeholder.
results: On 30 real-robot trials (a wheeled UGV reaching red/blue targets and a quadruped avoiding obstacles), DreamToNav succeeds in 23/30 (76.7%); per task this is 7/10, 8/10 and 8/10. Final discrepancy between plan and execution is about 0.05–0.10 m and tracking error is below 0.15 m over 2.3–2.9 m paths. No baseline is compared, so the results only show feasibility, not superiority over any other method.
limitations: Very small, simple evaluation: 3 short (<3 m) lab tasks, 30 trials, error metrics read approximately from plots, no baselines or ablations. Claimed abilities such as person following and social navigation are never evaluated.

Open-loop execution of a single dreamed trajectory with no replanning. Failures arise when the generated video misrepresents the scene layout or pose errors accumulate. Runtime and latency of video generation are not reported.
Requires a third-person image with the robot visible, known robot dimensions and camera intrinsics. Metric scale recovery from generated video via monocular ORB-SLAM3 is not addressed.
